c.tagline: West Africa's cultural crossroads, where Sahel meets savanna.

taxi.fareNote: Shared/private yellow taxis ('taxis jaunes') do not use meters; fares are negotiated with the driver before departure, so agree on the price upfront.

emergency.note: Response outside the capital is unreliable; in Ouagadougou call 17 (police) or 18 (fire/ambulance/SAMU); response times can still be slow, and many travelers rely on private clinics and their embassy for serious issues.

hood_landmark.Zone du Bois: Zone du Bois, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso

avoid.reason: Avoid the city outskirts and surroundings of government and military installations, and note most foreign governments advise against road travel outside the capital due to terrorism risk.
Motorbike bag-snatchers operate around the Grand Marché and Avenue Kwame Nkrumah; avoid walking after dark and stay alert in venues frequented by foreigners.

hood_desc: Modern southern district of wide boulevards, embassies and ministries, with the city's newest and most reliable hotels (backup generators, stable water/AC) - best for business travelers and those wanting comfort and security.

The historic downtown core along Avenue Kwame Nkrumah, next to the Grand Marché, banks and airline offices - walkable, central, and best for first-time visitors who want to be near sights and transit.
Leafy, low-density quarter long favored by NGO staff, diplomats and expats, packed with Lebanese and international restaurants - suits longer-stay visitors and those wanting a quieter, green base.

A central quartier in Secteur 4, immediately east of Avenue Kwame Nkrumah and the ZACA business zone; quiet residential streets within walking distance of downtown, suiting travellers who want the centre without the traffic of the main avenue.
A working-class western district around the main bus terminals for routes to Bobo-Dioulasso and beyond - convenient and cheap for overland travelers passing through or on tight budgets.

water.note: Tap water is unsafe; stick to bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor on board SOTRACO buses; there is no rechargeable transit card system. Most visitors instead rely on shared taxis or the Rapido ride-hailing app, paid in cash or via mobile money.
transit.hours: SOTRACO buses run roughly 6:00-20:00; taxis and Rapido operate later but night travel is best arranged in advance.
transit.note: Public buses are limited and not tourist-friendly; yellow shared/private taxis with negotiated fixed fares are the main way visitors get around.

train: SITARAIL passenger service to Bobo-Dioulasso, Banfora and Abidjan (Côte d'Ivoire), a few times weekly
bus: STAF, TCV and Rakieta (intercity coaches to Bobo-Dioulasso, Fada N'Gourma, and regional/international routes)

airport.name: Thomas Sankara International Airport (OUA)
airport.drive: 10-20 min from city center depending on traffic

tip.r: Tipping is not customary but rounding up or a small tip (5-10%) for good service at hotels/restaurants catering to travelers is appreciated, not expected.

landmarks: Grande Mosquée de Ouagadougou
This striking Sudano-Sahelian style mosque, built from mud-brick with distinctive wooden spikes, is one of the city's most photographed pieces of architecture.
Cathédrale de l'Immaculée Conception
Ouagadougou's principal Catholic cathedral impresses with its bold twin-towered facade, standing as a striking landmark in the heart of the capital.
Musée National du Burkina Faso
This open-air museum showcases traditional Burkinabé architecture through full-scale reconstructed ethnic huts alongside cultural artifacts and craftwork.
Monument des Martyrs
This soaring modern monument honors Burkina Faso's fallen heroes and has become a striking symbolic gathering point and photo landmark in the capital.
Siège du FESPACO
Headquarters of Africa's premier film festival, this building is a pilgrimage site for cinephiles celebrating Ouagadougou's status as the continent's film capital.
Village Artisanal de Ouagadougou
A bustling crafts village where visitors watch bronze casters, weavers, and leatherworkers at their trade while browsing vibrant handmade Burkinabé souvenirs.
Place des Nations Unies
A prominent roundabout and public square in the city center, this landmark plaza serves as a key civic gathering and orientation point.
Moro-Naba Palace
The traditional seat of the Mossi Emperor, this royal compound hosts a centuries-old Friday morning ceremony reenacting a legendary royal drama.
Ouagadougou Central Market district
The sprawling, colorful downtown market area pulses with vendors selling textiles, bronze art, and produce, offering an authentic taste of city life.
Kwame Nkrumah Avenue
The city's main commercial thoroughfare buzzes with shops, cafés, and street life, making it a popular starting point for exploring Ouagadougou.

train.note: Sitarail runs a passenger train about twice a week on the Burkinabe section only: Ouagadougou-Koudougou-Bobo-Dioulasso-Banfora-Niangoloko. The through international train to Abidjan (Cote d'Ivoire) has been suspended since 2023 pending Ivorian safety works. No online booking - buy tickets at Ouagadougou station.

intl.to: Abidjan (Cote d'Ivoire), Bamako (Mali), Lome (Togo), Accra (Ghana), Niamey (Niger) & Cotonou (Benin)

bus.note: International coaches leave from company yards near the Gare routiere / Ouaga-inter. Other major operators on these routes include TCV (Transport Confort Voyageurs), Rakieta and STAF; TCV's website was offline when checked, so buy at the terminal. Carry your passport and CFA cash for the borders.

ferry.note: Burkina Faso is landlocked - no ferries or boat services.

half.name: Bazoulé
half.blurb: Sacred crocodiles can be observed up close in a village pond about thirty kilometers southwest of Ouagadougou.

half.name: Laongo
half.blurb: An open-air granite sculpture site created by international artists sits roughly thirty-five kilometers east of Ouagadougou.

half.name: Ziniaré
half.blurb: A small Mossi town with a traditional royal court and a wildlife park lies about thirty-five kilometers northeast.
